title: 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' May Be Less a Film than a Vibe
author: Stephanie Zacharek
body:
It’s easy to feel nostalgia for the Hollywood filmmaking of the 1970s, when wily young directors succeeded in shaking the big-studio money tree to fund their outlandish, and often brilliant, projects. But we’ve also reached the era where the movies of the 1990s look pretty damn good. Which means David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is probably hitting at the right time. The script is by ’90s maverick Quentin Tarantino. The star is Brad Pitt, whose career has been off-and-on entwined with Fincher’s since the days of Seven and Fight Club. The story, a kind of sideways sequel to Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood, is set in Los Angeles in 1977, a time when the new Hollywood was bumping up against the old. To fans of ’70s Hollywood, and of Tarantino, Fincher, Pitt, or all three, the double nostalgia factor is almost irresistible, regardless of whether The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth hangs together as a movie.

And it doesn’t, quite. This is a meticulously shaggy piece of work, a movie stitched together from random stylish curlicues. To paraphrase the way Peter Fonda’s louche, rich-dude record-producer is described in Steven Soderbergh’s great 1999 Los Angeles noir The Limey, it’s not specific enough to be a movie; it’s more of a vibe. But sometimes a vibe is just the ticket, and the movie’s affection for a long-lost Los Angeles—not to mention its array of shabby-cool cars, of slithery white pant suits and French-cut T-shirts, of meticulously lacquered Farrah Fawcett-wannabe haircuts—is probably enough to carry it. Pitt reprises his Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood role as has-been stuntman Cliff Booth. His longtime colleague Rick Dalton (played, in Tarantino’s film, by Leonardo DiCaprio) has gone off to Australia to be a TV star there. Cliff is at loose ends, living way out in Marina Del Rey (for those not in the know, the geography of Los Angeles is helpfully explained in interstitial title cards) with his father, Gus (a gruffly charming Peter Weller), whom he adores—the two enjoy having a yak at the end of the day, building model fighter planes as they keep an eye on The Rockford Files.

Not that there’s ever an actual end to Cliff’s workday: he’s cobbled together a patchwork of odd jobs, including projecting films at the New Beverly Cinema, bartending at a lively tequila joint (the women patrons there love him, bellying up to the bar with invisible cartoon hearts shining in their eyes), and confronting the occasional criminal to clean up one mess or another. The movie opens with an elaborately staged sequence, capped with a blast of violence and an unsentimental act of mercy, in which Cliff protects the secret of a Hollywood bigwig with a penchant for picking up young male cuties. Cliff will take a dirty job here and here, but he also has principles. And though he never spells it out, he’d love to get back to stuntwork.

That’s why he’s intrigued when he gets a phone message—it comes through on his 1970s-style answering machine, which is about the size of a small Buick—from an agent, Elizabeth Debicki’s Karen Crosby (no relation to Bing, though that possibility becomes one of the movie’s many frothy, tossed-off jokes). She wants him to meet with her client, Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a pugilistic and very short TV star who insists on doing his own stunts and whom nobody seems to like. It turns out Charlie needs help calming down a couple of thugs he met while making a movie in the Philippines—they’re played by Matt Groove and JB Tadena—and he thinks Cliff can help. Meanwhile, Cliff has his eye on the sultry-smart Crosby—he’d never call her by her first name—though she resists his half-scrappy, half-laid-back charm offensive. Because she’s the kind of woman you have to earn.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth leap-frogs from one misadventure to another with entropic grace. Here and there it hits a false note: those Filipino thugs commit a murderous act that’s designed to show us what true baddies they are, and its excessive brutality feels like your typical instance of Tarantino overkill. Overall, though, the Tarantino-Fincher-Pitt mashup throws off plenty of amiable energy. (It was Pitt who brought screenwriter and director together, after Tarantino opted against directing the film himself.) Fincher, ever the perfectionist, and cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt (who won an Oscar for his work on Fincher’s now nearly forgotten Mank) give the movie just the right level of gritty polish, as if they’d been saving up some of the hazy, moody sunbeams of The Long Goodbye in a jar, waiting for just the right use. And Fincher has assembled a lively constellation of actors to revolve around Pitt, the movie’s raffish sun king, including Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as blaxploitation star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison and Carla Gugino as Charlie’s wife, Toni, who’s so spikily appealing she could anchor her own spinoff.

And Pitt is great fun to watch here: As Cliff sniffs the armpits of every tiki-surfer shirt he owns, in search of the one that still smells OK, you get a sense of a guy who knows that being cool actually burns a great deal of energy. He’s always on the move, but you can also see him longing for a place to land. There’s something wistful about him—he’s the guy who can’t have everything he wants and has learned to be thrilled with the leftovers. Pitt captures all of that, especially when he gazes at Crosby’s face, a fortress of resistance that can’t be broken down by his barrage of drawling wisecracks.

The most significant flaw of The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is that it doesn’t allow Cliff and Crosby their moment of romantic rapprochement. It’s almost as if Fincher and Tarantino were actively resisting the pleasurable release a great romantic comedy can give us. (Tarantino knew better when he made his greatest film, Jackie Brown.) Do they just think that stuff is too girly? Regardless, they do seem to know what a treasure they have in Debicki. Pitt is perfectly likable, but she’s the movie's secret star. As Crosby, she’s the kind of girl those 1970s bias-cut skirts were made for—she makes her entrance in a lean column of silky eggshell crepe that seems to go on forever. (The costumes here are by Trish Summerville.) Debicki knows just what to hide and what to reveal with a character like this. She’s a woman who knows her heart can be broken, which is why she guards it so carefully. For every secret she unreels for Cliff—in a past life she was a film critic for a small-town newspaper, a job she landed after her idol, New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael, put in a good word for her—you know there are a hundred more that will never leave the vault. Debicki says it all with her eyes: she wants to break free, but she needs to be careful.

One of the movie's finest throwaway moments is a simple sequence of Variety magazine party pics showing various luminaries at a Hollywood premiere. Debicki’s Crosby is there among them, not a star but still a standout. We see her lurking in a corner, dressed in a tall-drink-of-water white pantsuit, lifting a cigarette to her lips. In some shots, she’s glancing sideways with half-closed eyes. If she were a celebrity, photographs like these would be outtakes; as it is, she’s just an attractive party attendee, certainly striking, but not yet a Hollywood somebody.

Hollywood is a place where insecurity hangs in the air like Yves Saint Laurent’s Opium, oppressive and unmissable. But Crosby, as Debicki plays her, stands clear of those fumes. She shows us that vulnerability isn’t the same as insecurity, and she’s probably too good for Cliff Booth, as disreputably dazzling as he is. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth reconstructs Los Angeles as it was in 1977, or at least as it exists in our dreams, a place where art deco movie palaces and cheap hamburger joints make easy neighbors. Crosby is the emblem of that dream and its contradictions. She may be a nobody, but she’s her own somebody. And without even trying, she walks off with the film as if it were her name in the title.
